active molecules and also serve as indispensable substrates for a wide range
of stereospecific reactions afording sp<sup>3</sup>-hybridized skeletons. However,
there is a persisting lack of methods that generate the thermodynamically
less stable Z-isomers. Here we report an iron-catalysed multicomponent
strategy that merges allenes, dialkylzinc compounds and haloalkanes to
construct trisubstituted alkenes with excellent control of regioselectivity
and Z-selectivity. Selective installation of diverse C(sp<sup>3</sup>) groups enables
access to a broad library of functionalized unsaturated products. The
synthetic utility of the method is highlighted through the synthesis of a
glucosylceramide synthase inhibitor. Contrary to conventional mechanisms
for metal-catalysed allene functionalization, our studies suggest a
kinetically controlled pathway involving sequential radical-mediated
alkylferration of the less hindered C=C bond and inner-sphere alkylation via
reductive elimination. Mechanistic and computational investigations reveal
the origins of the stereochemical outcome.

in any chemical transformation that aims to synthesize unsymmetric

forms<sup>7,8</sup>. This challenge is even greater in the context of acyclic all-
carbon trisubstituted alkenes due to greater steric hindrance and the
small energy gap between the Z- and E-isomers<sup>9</sup> (Fig. 1a). Unsurpris-
ingly, limited progress has been made in this area in the past decade.

or nickel-mediated carbometallation pathways<sup>29–31</sup> that deliver
π-systems as stereoisomeric mixtures or predominantly E-isomers
(via π-allyl intermediates). Deviating from this approach and in the
presence of an appropriate ligated iron complex i and an alkylmetal
nucleophile 2, we envisioned a mechanistically distinct pathway involv-
ing in situ generation of an alkyl iron species ii that could preferentially
react with the less substituted π-bond of allene 1 through site-selective
radical-based alkylferration<sup>32</sup>. The resulting alkenyl iron intermediate
iii, which could exist either in the Z- or E-isomeric form, then undergoes
C–C coupling with a haloalkane electrophile 3 to give the trisubstituted
alkene product 4. To facilitate formation of the desired but energetically
disfavoured Z-4, we reasoned that Z-iii must be selectively formed under
kinetic control. Furthermore, stereoretentive alkylation of Z-iii with 3
must be faster than any adventitious isomerization of Z-iii to E-iii. Added
to these uncertainties is the susceptibility of allene 1 towards radical
additions at the C1, C2 or C3 positions, and attack at the sp-hybridized
central carbon (C2) to form resonance-stabilized allylic radicals is usu-
ally more favoured<sup>33</sup>. This implies that the radical-mediated alkylferra-
tion step has to overcome the intrinsic substrate reactivity to achieve
high regioselectivity for alkyl radical addition at C1. Here we disclose the
successful realization of an iron-catalysed allene dialkylation strategy
to generate all-carbon trisubstituted Z-alkenes with exquisite control
of site and stereoselectivities (Fig. 1d).

Results and discussion
Reaction optimization
The three-component union of allene 5, diethyl zinc 6 and prenyl bro-
mide 7 was investigated to identify optimal reaction conditions (Sup-
plementary Table 1). Specifically, various Fe(II) and Fe(III) complexes,
and a range of ligands, were surveyed for 1,2-dialkylation in the presence
of tetrahydrofuran (THF) as solvent at 60 °C (Table 1). In the absence of
ligand, the best results were obtained using 10 mol% of FeBr (entry 2),
which afforded the desired trisubstituted alkene 8 in 67% yield and 90:10
Z:E ratio as the sole regioisomer. The configuration of the major Z-isomer
was confirmed by nuclear Overhauser effect spectroscopy. Although
there was minimal formation of 9 or 10 (from dialkylation of the more
substituted C=C bond of 5), small amounts of 11 (from non-selective
hydroalkylation of 5 with 7) and 12 (from non-selective dialkylation
of 5 with 7) were detected as by-products. These results highlight the
complexity and difficulty of orchestrating selective additions of two
different aliphatic groups to allenyl substrates featuring cumulated
diene structures (versus alkenes which only possess a single C=C bond).

Reaction scope and synthetic application
The generality of the iron-catalysed reaction conditions was first
assessed by examining various functionalized allenes (Fig. 2). Aryl- and
heteroaryl-substituted allenes with electron-rich or electron-deficient
substituents were successfully transformed to the corresponding
skipped dienes (8, 14–25), prevalent motifs in natural products<sup>34,35</sup>,
in 52–70% yield with complete regioselectivity and good to excellent
Z-selectivity across the board. These include products that contain an
amine (16), a halogen (17), a carboxylic ester (18), a thiophene and ben-
zothiophene (23, 24), and a ferrocene (25). Slightly diminished stere-
oselectivities were obtained for allenes that bear sterically demanding
groups (20, 24, 25). 1,2-Dialkylation of N-substituted allenes delivered
trisubstituted enamines 26 and 27. Of particular note, 1,1-disubstituted
allenes could also undergo reaction to furnish tetrasubstituted alkenes
(28–30), which are typically challenging to prepare due to steric hin-
drance. However, poor conversions were observed with trisubstituted
allene 31 and less-activated alkyl-substituted allene substrates 32 and
33. Access to 8 and 14–28 underscores the ease of introducing prenyl
groups through our catalytic approach, which is relevant in protein
and biomolecule settings<sup>36,37</sup>.

ophiles in the multicomponent system (Fig. 3). In general, allylic and

position to construct trisubstituted Z-alkenes (Fig. 3b).

(ref. 38). It is worth mentioning that switching the Z-alkene configura-
tion in 59 to the E-isomer led to reduced bioactivity, underscoring the
value of our Z-selective dialkylation reaction.

Conclusions
Three-component 1,2-dialkylation of allenes was attained using a bis-
phosphine–iron catalyst to assemble stereodefined trisubstituted
alkenes. Various aliphatic groups could be installed with simultaneous
control of site and Z-selectivities. Mechanistic and computational find-
ings suggest a unique mechanism involving radical-mediated alkylfer-
ration followed by inner-sphere C–C bond formation, offering critical
insights for designing kinetically controlled transformations of allenes
and other π-systems. We anticipate the widespread adoption of this
chemistry as a practical tool for constructing value-added unsaturated
motifs to facilitate applications in complex molecule synthesis.
Methods
General procedure for iron-catalysed 1,2-dialkylation of allenes
In a nitrogen-filled glovebox, an oven-dried 4.0 ml vial equipped with
a magnetic stir bar was charged with FeBr (10 mol%), ligand (12 mol%),
alkyl bromide (2.0 equiv.) and allene (0.1 mmol, 1.0 equiv.) in THF
(0.4 ml). Dialkylzinc (2.0 equiv.) was then slowly added into the system.
The vial was sealed and removed from the glovebox, and the reaction
mixture was allowed to stir at 60 °C for 8 h. After cooling to ambient
temperature, the crude mixture was purified by silica gel chromatog-
raphy to give the desired product.
